name: Augment Code
summary: A commercial coding agent for VS Code, JetBrains and the terminal built around a Context Engine that keeps a live semantic index of your codebase. On 8 October 2026 Harness bought the Context Engine, the Auggie CLI and the Cosmos cloud agents.
intro: Augment’s difference is retrieval. When you open a workspace, the extension uploads your code to Augment’s cloud and its Context Engine builds a search index for you alone: an embedding index, kept per developer so it follows your branch, that Augment says updates within seconds of a change. Embeddings are computed and searched on Augment’s own infrastructure rather than through third-party APIs, and a proof-of-possession check means you can only retrieve code you actually have locally. `.gitignore` and `.augmentignore` decide what gets indexed. The agent in VS Code and JetBrains (chat and completions also exist for Vim and Neovim) uses that index to pull the relevant code even from monorepos of more than 100,000 files, then edits files, runs terminal commands, calls MCP servers and native integrations such as GitHub, Jira and Linear, and keeps checkpoints you can roll back to.

Auggie, the CLI launched in September 2025, puts the same agent and index in the terminal: an interactive TUI, `auggie --print` for scripts and CI, an ACP mode for Zed, Neovim and Emacs, and an MCP server mode that hands the Context Engine to other agents such as Claude Code, Codex or Cursor. Cosmos runs agents in cloud or self-hosted sandboxes, triggered by tickets, pull requests or alerts. You choose the model (Claude, GPT, Gemini, Kimi, GLM and others) and pay the provider’s list price plus a 40% service fee. On 8 October 2026 Harness bought Cosmos, the Auggie CLI, the Code Context Engine and related technology, and the team behind them moved to Harness. The VS Code and JetBrains extensions were still getting releases when the deal was announced.
strengths: Retrieval built for large codebases: a per-developer index that follows branch switches within seconds, across several repositories
The Context Engine is usable outside Augment: Auggie’s MCP server mode gives other agents its codebase search
Enterprise controls: SOC 2 Type II, ISO/IEC 42001, customer-managed keys, and no training on customer code
One agent across VS Code, JetBrains, the terminal, CI and cloud sandboxes
limits: Ownership is in flux: Harness bought the Context Engine, the Auggie CLI and Cosmos in October 2026, and the announcements say nothing about the future of the IDE extensions
Indexing uploads your code to Augment’s cloud, and retrieval runs there rather than on your machine
Closed source and paid only, with a 40% fee on top of model list prices; pricing moved from per-message plans to credits in October 2025 and then to token-based billing
Tool permission rules are enforced by the CLI and Cosmos but not by the IDE extension
Its published quality gains, such as 30 to 80% better results for agents using the Context Engine MCP, come from Augment’s own benchmarks

sections.title: What it costs (checked 2026-10-09)
sections.intro: Augment bills in dollars of usage. Every request costs the model’s tokens at the provider’s public list price, plus a service fee, plus sandbox time when Cosmos runs it.

rows.label: Standard
values: $20 of usage included, up to 50 seats, no per-seat charge

rows.label: Business
values: $100 of usage included, up to 50 seats

rows.label: Service fee
values: Funds the Context Engine and Cosmos; no fee on compute

rows.label: Enterprise
values: SSO, SCIM, customer-managed keys, unlimited users

notes: From Augment’s pricing page and token-based pricing docs, checked on 2026-10-09, the day after the Harness deal was announced.

story: Augment was founded by Igor Ostrovsky, formerly chief architect at Pure Storage and an engineer at Microsoft, and Guy Gur-Ari, an AI researcher from Google, with Scott Dietzen as CEO. It came out of stealth on 24 April 2024 with a $227 million Series B at a $977 million valuation, $252 million in total. Its pitch was that existing assistants didn’t understand a programmer’s intent or a team’s code. It built its own indexing and retrieval rather than calling generic embedding APIs.

The product grew from completions and chat into Augment Agent for VS Code and JetBrains in April 2025, with memories, MCP and native integrations, and then the Auggie CLI in September 2025. Heavy agent use broke its pricing: in October 2025 Augment said one user on the $250 Max plan was costing it close to $15,000 a month, and moved from per-message plans to credits, and later to token-based billing. In February 2026 it opened the Context Engine to other agents over MCP, and it built Cosmos to run fleets of agents from tickets, reviews and alerts.

On 8 October 2026 Harness, a software delivery platform company, announced it had acquired select Augment Code assets: Cosmos, the Auggie CLI, the Code Context Engine and related technology. The team behind them, including co-founder and CTO Igor Ostrovsky, joined Harness, and Cosmos became the Harness Cosmos Software Factory Agent.

choices.choice: Build its own indexing and embedding search
choices.why: Augment argued that generic embedding APIs plus a hosted vector database gave poor quality, slow updates and a security risk, since embeddings can be reversed into code. Running its own models on its own infrastructure let it update a per-developer index within seconds.

choices.choice: One index per developer, not per repository
choices.why: Developers switch branches and rebase all the time. Retrieving from the main branch, or from an index refreshed every 10 minutes, feeds the model names that don’t exist in the code being edited.
A shared cloud index could leak code to people who shouldn’t see it. Requiring the client to prove it holds the code avoids managing per-file permissions.

choices.choice: Expose the Context Engine to other agents
choices.why: Many teams already used Claude Code, Cursor or Codex. Offering the index over MCP let those agents use Augment’s retrieval, which Augment said improved their results by 30 to 80% in its own tests.
